observation: Extreme rotation measure of order 1e5 rad m^-2 with ~10 percent decline over about 7 months, and near-100 percent linear polarization
locator: Reported observed RM ~1.46e5 rad m^-2 (Jan 2017) falling to ~1.33e5 (Aug 2017); exact source-frame value depends on the (1+z)^2 correction, verify against source
hypothesis: Magnetar in a dense, highly magnetized nebula or near a massive black hole
confidence_note: RM magnitude and its secular decline are robust; the physical identification of the Faraday screen is a model-dependent inference, not a measurement
unresolved_ambiguity: A compact magnetized nebula and a supermassive-black-hole environment both reproduce the RM magnitude; the data do not separate them

observation: Continued secular decline of the rotation measure over multiple years, roughly a factor of a few, without a sign change
locator: RM decline tracked with Effelsberg and Arecibo; decline rate quoted as roughly 15 percent per year at the time, verify exact rate against source
hypothesis: Expanding or evolving magneto-ionic screen local to the source, e.g. a young supernova remnant or magnetar wind nebula
confidence_note: The trend is well sampled; attributing it to expansion rather than to line-of-sight motion through a structured screen is interpretation
unresolved_ambiguity: Screen expansion, orbital motion, and turbulent screen crossing all predict monotonic-looking decline over a few-year baseline

observation: Rotation measure reversed sign twice within about a year, swinging through zero between values of order +/-1e4 rad m^-2
locator: Sign reversals reported from FAST and GBT monitoring; exact endpoint RM values uncertain here, verify against source
hypothesis: Neutron star in a binary with a magnetized wind from a massive or degenerate companion
confidence_note: The sign reversal itself is a direct measurement and is hard to produce with a static nebula; the binary interpretation is one of several
unresolved_ambiguity: A binary companion wind, a turbulent nebula with reversing field, and a supernova-remnant filament crossing all remain viable

observation: Irregular rotation measure variation of order several hundred rad m^-2 over weeks followed by a plateau, together with circular polarization reaching tens of percent in some bursts
locator: FAST monitoring campaign; peak circular polarization fraction quoted as high (up to ~75 percent in the paper as recalled), value uncertain, verify against source
hypothesis: Magnetospheric propagation or conversion in a dynamic, magnetized circumburst medium
confidence_note: RM variability is securely measured; circular polarization can arise both in the magnetosphere and from propagation, so the site is not fixed by this datum
unresolved_ambiguity: Generalized Faraday conversion in a magnetized plasma screen versus intrinsic magnetospheric circular polarization

observation: Linear polarization fraction falls with decreasing frequency across several repeaters, consistent with multipath RM scatter in a turbulent screen
locator: Depolarization parametrized by an RM scatter term; larger scatter associated with larger and more variable RM
hypothesis: Repeaters sit in dense, turbulent, magnetized environments
confidence_note: The frequency dependence is a population-level empirical trend; sample size is small and selection toward bright, well-monitored repeaters is severe
unresolved_ambiguity: Whether the depolarizing screen is source-local or an unrelated foreground is not settled per source

observation: Diverse polarization position angle swings within individual bursts, including swings of tens of degrees across a single burst
locator: FAST detection of varied PA swings across a burst sample from one repeater
hypothesis: Magnetospheric emission from a rotating neutron star (rotating-vector-like geometry)
confidence_note: The PA swings are measured; the rotating-vector-model reading is an interpretation contested in the literature (see the PA-swing disagreement record)
unresolved_ambiguity: Swings can be produced by magnetospheric geometry or by structure in a relativistic shock; this observation alone does not decide

observation: Flat, essentially constant polarization position angle within and between bursts at high frequency, with near-100 percent linear polarization
locator: PA reported as constant across bursts after RM correction
hypothesis: Magnetospheric emission from a rotating neutron star
confidence_note: A flat PA is compatible with magnetospheric emission viewed along a favourable geometry and also with shock models; it is not by itself discriminating
unresolved_ambiguity: Flat PA and swinging PA occur in different repeaters, so PA behaviour is not a clean class marker

observation: Smooth S-shaped polarization position angle swing of order 100 degrees within a single burst from an apparent non-repeater
locator: CHIME/FRB detection; swing amplitude quoted as ~130 degrees as recalled, verify amplitude and reference details against source
hypothesis: Magnetospheric emission from a rotating neutron star, extended to apparent non-repeaters
confidence_note: Reference details are from recall and should be re-checked before being relied on; the measurement, if confirmed as described, is a direct pulsar-like analogue
unresolved_ambiguity: Whether one PA-swinging non-repeater generalizes to the non-repeating population is untested

observation: Scintillation analysis of a single burst used to bound the transverse size of the emission region to a scale far smaller than a shock radius
locator: Two-screen scintillation argument; the quoted emitting-region bound is small (order 1e4 km or less as recalled), value uncertain, verify against source
hypothesis: Magnetospheric (close-in) emission rather than far-away relativistic shock
confidence_note: If the two-screen geometry holds, this is among the most direct size constraints available; the constraint is only as good as the screen-distance assumptions
unresolved_ambiguity: Screen distances are inferred, not measured; a different screen configuration relaxes the size bound

observation: Periodic activity window with a period of 16.35 days, with bursts confined to roughly a five-day phase window at 400-800 MHz
locator: Period reported as 16.35 +/- 0.15 days from CHIME/FRB monitoring
hypothesis: Binary orbital modulation of a neutron star by a companion wind or by beam obscuration
confidence_note: The periodicity is a robust timing result; the mechanism producing the window is not measured
unresolved_ambiguity: Orbital modulation, free precession of a magnetar, and ultra-slow rotation all fit a 16-day window

observation: The activity window shifts in phase and changes width with observing frequency, arriving later and lasting longer at low frequency
citation: Pastor-Marazuela et al. 2021, Nature 596, 505; Pleunis et al. 2021, ApJL 911, L3
locator: Apertif ~1.4 GHz versus LOFAR 110-188 MHz activity phases compared
hypothesis: Binary orbital modulation with a frequency-dependent absorbing or refracting wind
confidence_note: The chromatic shift is measured in two independent low-frequency datasets; the absorption interpretation is model-dependent
unresolved_ambiguity: A frequency-dependent window can arise from a stratified binary wind or from an intrinsically frequency-dependent emission geometry in a precessing magnetosphere

observation: Candidate periodic activity cycle of roughly 157 days, with a duty cycle of order half
locator: Period reported near 157 days from archival activity; later analyses have revised the value (a ~161-day value has been reported), so treat the exact period as unsettled
hypothesis: Long-period modulation of a repeater by an orbit or by precession
confidence_note: Derived from heterogeneous archival monitoring with strong sampling windows; the significance is far weaker than for FRB 20180916B
unresolved_ambiguity: Period value, and whether the modulation is real rather than an artifact of observing cadence, are both open

observation: Nine sub-bursts spanning about three seconds with a regular spacing of 216.8 ms, i.e. sub-second periodicity within one burst
locator: Periodicity significance reported at the ~6.5 sigma level for a single event
hypothesis: A rotating neutron star with a spin period of ~0.2 s, favouring a compact-object rotator over a shock-driven one-off
confidence_note: A single event; the detection is statistically solid but has not been repeated in another source at comparable significance
unresolved_ambiguity: Whether 216.8 ms is the rotation period, a harmonic of it, or a quasi-periodic magnetospheric oscillation is not determined

observation: No periodicity found in a sample of 1652 bursts from one repeater over timescales from about 1 ms to 1000 s
locator: FAST campaign, 1652 bursts in 59.5 hours; peak rate reported as ~122 bursts per hour
hypothesis: Rotationally modulated magnetar with a detectable spin period
confidence_note: A negative result, first-class as evidence; sensitive only to periodicities within the searched range and to bursts above the detection threshold
unresolved_ambiguity: Absence of spin periodicity may mean no rotational gating, a period outside the search range, or emission from many magnetospheric locations

observation: Sub-bursts drift downward in frequency with time within a burst envelope, the so-called sad-trombone effect
locator: Complex time-frequency structure characterized at 1.4-5 GHz
hypothesis: Emission from a radius-to-frequency-mapped magnetosphere, or from a decelerating shock
confidence_note: The drift is a secure and now widely reproduced empirical signature; both major emission frameworks have produced drift models
unresolved_ambiguity: Downward drifting is predicted by both magnetospheric radius-to-frequency mapping and by shock deceleration, so it is not discriminating as usually applied

observation: Repeater bursts are on average narrower in bandwidth and longer in duration than apparent non-repeater bursts
citation: Pleunis et al. 2021, ApJL 923, L1; CHIME/FRB Collaboration 2021, ApJS 257, 59
locator: Morphological classification of the first CHIME/FRB catalog
hypothesis: Repeaters and apparent non-repeaters are physically distinct populations or distinct emission states
confidence_note: The morphological difference is statistically established within one instrument's band and selection function; instrumental selection is not fully removed
unresolved_ambiguity: The difference may reflect two progenitor classes, two emission states of one class, or beaming and viewing-angle differences

observation: Highly polarized microstructure resolved down to microsecond timescales in a repeater
locator: Coherent-dedispersion VLBI-style observations resolving microshots
hypothesis: A compact, magnetospheric-scale emission region rather than a large shock front
confidence_note: The timescale measurement is direct; converting it to an emission size requires assumptions about relativistic beaming and coherence
unresolved_ambiguity: Microsecond structure can be imposed by the emitter or by propagation and lensing along the path

observation: Microsecond-scale burst structure and low burst luminosities in a repeater located in a globular cluster
citation: Nimmo et al. 2022, Nature Astronomy 6, 393; Kirsten et al. 2022, Nature 602, 585
locator: Short timescales and luminosities that overlap the pulsar/magnetar regime
hypothesis: Neutron star from an old-population formation channel (globular cluster, not core collapse)
confidence_note: The environment and the short timescales are both well established; the emission mechanism is not fixed by either
unresolved_ambiguity: Whether this low-luminosity, old-environment source belongs to the same phenomenon as cosmological FRBs is genuinely open

observation: Burst energy distribution is bimodal rather than a single power law, over a large single-source sample
locator: 1652 bursts from FAST; bimodality reported in isotropic-equivalent energy
hypothesis: A single scale-free magnetospheric avalanche process producing all bursts
confidence_note: The bimodality is measured with high burst counts but is entangled with the detection threshold and with the source being in a high-activity state
unresolved_ambiguity: Bimodality may reflect two emission mechanisms, two magnetospheric regions, or a threshold-plus-saturation artifact

observation: A Galactic magnetar produced a millisecond radio burst with energy far below the weakest known extragalactic FRB, accompanied by a hard X-ray burst
citation: CHIME/FRB Collaboration 2020, Nature 587, 54; Bochenek et al. 2020, Nature 587, 59; Mereghetti et al. 2020, ApJL 898, L29
locator: Radio burst detected at 400-800 MHz and at 1.4 GHz with a contemporaneous hard X-ray burst
hypothesis: Magnetars produce FRB-like bursts, but a single magnetar population must span a very wide energy range
confidence_note: The radio and X-ray association is secure; the energy gap to cosmological FRBs is large and its size depends on distance assumptions for the magnetar
unresolved_ambiguity: Whether one luminosity function spans Galactic magnetar bursts and cosmological FRBs, or whether two source classes are involved, is unresolved
